To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) large conductance potassium channels are activated in medial vestibular neurons during spontaneous activity and are regulated by Ca(2+)/ calmodulin-dependent kinase and protein kinase C, and 2) the regulation of these channels is bidirectional.
BK channels in medial vestibular neurons are modulated by CAMKII via a shift in voltage activation range, and that PKC modulates the open probability of these channels.
large conductance Ca(2+) activated potassium (BK) channels in the medial vestibular nucleus (MNV) are modulated by protein kinase C (PKG) and Ca(2+)/Calmodulin-dependent kinase (CAMKII).

the mechanisms by which neurons regulate their excitability and the consequences of these changes for neuronal function.

the role of large conductance calcium-activated potassium channels in regulating neuronal excitability and plasticity in the medial vestibular nucleus, a key brainstem structure involved in the vestibulo-oculomotor reflex.
the mechanisms that regulate the intrinsic excitability of neurons and how this regulation is affected by the activity of kinases.

CAMKII and protein kinase C (PKG) have opposing roles in regulating the open probability of BK channels.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

BK channels in MVN neurons are bidirectionally controlled by CAMKII (increase) and PKC (decrease) in the range of membrane potentials over which they are activated, and that this control is likely mediated by direct interactions with the BK channel complex.
the bidirectional control of large conductance potassium channels by CAMK II and PKC may be important in regulating neuronal excitability and plasticity in the medial vestibular nucleus.
BK channel open probability is regulated by CAMKII/PKC in a bidirectional manner, and this regulation is likely to play a role in vestibular plasticity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the activity of BK channels in neurons is dynamically regulated by kinases.

the open probability of large conductance potassium (BK) channels is bidirectionally controlled by Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CAMKI) and protein kinase C (PKG) in medial vestibular neuron.
the open probability of BK channels in MVN neurons can be modulated by kinetically distinct mechanisms that shift the activation range of BK channels in opposing directions.
